anchor: Love seeketh not itself to please
title: The Clod and the Pebble: context and allusion
short: A poem from Songs of Experience (1794) in which two speakers give opposite definitions of love; the clod's song echoes St Paul's hymn to charity.
body: The clod's first line echoes 1 Corinthians 13:5, where charity (love) 'seeketh not her own'. The clod speaks for self-sacrificing love; the pebble for possessive, selfish love. The poem is one of the Songs of Experience, Blake's companion volume to the Songs of Innocence (1789), which show 'the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul'. Its three quatrains, mostly of four-stress lines, use a frame (the middle stanza) that introduces each speaker in turn.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, 1 Corinthians 13:4-7
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
Geoffrey Keynes, ed., Songs of Innocence and of Experience (Oxford UP, 1970), introduction and commentary

anchor: builds a heaven in hell's despair
title: Heaven in hell, hell in heaven
short: The two refrains echo Satan's claim in Paradise Lost that the mind 'can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven'.
body: In Paradise Lost 1.254-255 Satan says that the mind 'in itself / Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven'. Blake divides the line between two speakers: the clod's love builds heaven even in hell's despair; the pebble's builds hell 'in heaven's despite'. Blake admired Milton but believed that Milton's Satan expresses energy and desire, as he argued in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. The allusion suggests that both kinds of love are acts of the mind that make the world they live in.

sources.cite: John Milton, Paradise Lost 1.254-255 (Dartmouth Milton Reading Room)
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
Harold Bloom, Blake's Apocalypse (1963)

title: The clod of clay
short: The clod, soft and 'Trodden with the cattle's feet', yields to pressure and takes the shape of what crushes it: an emblem of self-abnegation.
body: Clay also suggests the human body, made from dust (Genesis 2:7), and passive, malleable humility. The clod's selflessness is admirable, yet it is trodden down. Some readers think Blake shows that selfless love is purchased by being trampled, and is perhaps a kind of martyrdom or masochism. In Blake's earlier Book of Thel (1789), the 'Clod of Clay' appears as a figure of humble, maternal love.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Genesis 2:7
William Blake, The Book of Thel (1789), plates 4-5
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom

title: The pebble of the brook
short: The pebble, hard and smoothed by running water, is untouched and unchanged by its surroundings: an emblem of a self-contained ego.
body: A stone in a brook is polished by the water but never yields. The pebble 'Warbled', a word for birdsong, so its selfish creed has its own sweetness and confidence. A biblical echo may be present: David chose 'five smooth stones out of the brook' to kill Goliath (1 Samuel 17:40). Clod and pebble are both earth, differing only in softness, which supports readings in which their two creeds are aspects of one nature.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, 1 Samuel 17:40
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
Geoffrey Keynes, ed., Songs of Innocence and of Experience (Oxford UP, 1970), introduction and commentary

title: metres meet
short: 'Meet' means fitting or suitable: the pebble sings verses appropriate to it.
body: 'Meet' is an archaic adjective meaning proper or apt, familiar from the Prayer Book ('It is meet and right so to do'). The phrase draws attention to the poem's own metres: the two songs are metrically parallel, and the pebble's echoes the clod's line by line, inverting its sense. The shift from the clod's 'sang' to the pebble's 'Warbled' may be a slight judgment, or simply variety.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v.
The Book of Common Prayer (1662), Holy Communion ('It is meet and right so to do')

anchor: To bind another to its delight
title: Binding love
short: The pebble's love binds the beloved to its own pleasure: possessive love is a form of imprisonment, a central concern in Songs of Experience.
body: Binding is one of Blake's key images for repression and control: priests 'binding with briars my joys and desires' in 'The Garden of Love', and the 'mind-forg'd manacles' of 'London'. The pebble's love takes pleasure in another's 'loss of ease'. Yet the pebble is honest about desire, while the clod may be self-deceived; this is why critics debate whether Blake prefers either.

sources.cite: David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
Harold Bloom, Blake's Apocalypse (1963)
William Blake, 'London' and 'The Garden of Love', Songs of Experience (1794)

anchor: builds a hell in heaven's despite
title: in heaven's despite
short: 'In despite of' means in contempt or defiance of: the pebble's love builds hell in defiance of heaven.
body: 'Despite' as a noun means scorn, contempt, or malice. The rhyme with 'delight' (l. 10) binds the pebble's pleasure to spite. The final line mirrors the first stanza's 'heaven in hell's despair' with a chiastic reversal: despair becomes despite, heaven and hell exchange places. The symmetry makes the poem seem a balanced debate without a verdict. Blake often uses such exact verbal mirroring in the Songs, as in the paired 'Holy Thursday' and 'Nurse's Song' poems of Innocence and Experience.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v.
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom

title: Contraries: which is right?
short: Blake gives no verdict. Critics read the poem as a satire on selfish love, a critique of both, or a demonstration of Blake's 'Contraries'.
body: In The Marriage of Heaven and Hell Blake wrote 'Without Contraries is no progression'. Some readers take the clod as right and the pebble as the voice of Experience corrupting love. Others note that the clod's self-sacrifice is the morality Blake elsewhere criticises as self-annihilating and passive, and that the pebble at least knows what it wants. A third reading is that each love is partial: true love would integrate self and other. The placement in Songs of Experience suggests both voices belong to a fallen state.

sources.cite: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (c. 1790), plate 3
Harold Bloom, Blake's Apocalypse (1963)
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
